Stale-binary detector built (scripts/check_stale_binaries.ps1) and, in the course of verifying it, measured something that changes how .ex5 evidence can be read at all: MQL5 compilation is NOT byte-deterministic. The order asked for hash mismatch between copies to be reported as a fault; obeying that literally would have manufactured 111 false findings every day - a brand-new detector engineered to be muted inside a week, which is the exact failure ORDER-218 had just finished documenting. Downgraded to HASH_DIFFERS, advisory, never fails the run. The ORDER-213 hash-in-README precedent survives untouched because it compares one file to itself across a copy, not one build to another build. Scope turned out to be the whole job: pointing the roaming root at Terminal\* found 1313 binaries across 27 terminal folders and 530 findings, of which 709 had no source in this repo (bought/downloaded EAs) and 502 were hash noise from dead installs - 530 findings is not a detector, it is a wall. Default is now the four places a binary can actually be attached or tested from with the live terminal id pinned, giving 209 records and a readable STALE 28. Known Boss_16 case reproduced exactly, naming all 7 newer core .mqh files rather than emitting a bare stale line - the bare line is what got ignored on 07-25. Wrote the triage into the script header because a STALE line is not self-interpreting: tpl_regression recompiles via deploy.ps1 -Compile before every run so its stale test binaries are cosmetic, while anything attached to a chart without a rebuild is the real exposure; and mtime is itself weak because git checkout rewrites it, so the newer files must be confirmed as EDITED (spot-checked: the 7 core files are genuine ORDER-187/194 edits of 07-24, not checkout artifacts). Re-ran the lot-mode cage so its unit-independence claim rests on a real sample. Why E always dies, which the order did not state: E is D's ratio expressed 10x SMALLER, and 0.20 lot on a $2,000 deposit is ten times the risk of 0.20 lot on $20,000, so the 25% DD kill fires and the run ends at 6 trades in 8 days. The first-lot assertion still held (the first deal precedes any kill) but a PASS that does not say how thin it is can be read as more than it is. Chose to ADD a leg rather than enlarge E: E stays, because it is the honest statement of the limit - a fixed ratio means equally SIZED, not equally SURVIVABLE - and E2_unit_indep_hi runs the same ratio 10x LARGER (anchor 100000 / deposit 200000) where the kill cannot reach. Result: D(x1) E(x0.1) E2(x10) all size 0.20, so unit-independence now holds across 100x of absolute size, and E2 is a full 164-trade window confirmed from its own truncation sidecar rather than by eye. The order did not ask for this and it matters more: entry 16 carried the identical debt, and entry 16 is what is queued for a demo chart. K1_scaled_1x AND K1_scaled_2x were BOTH killed (eqDD 25.09 / 25.03, 59 trades each), so _16_BaseLotMode's evidence was two truncated runs compared against each other - they agree, but about a shortened window. Added K1_scaled_hi at deposit 200000: 71 trades, full window, same 0.20 lot. 71 is exactly K0-flat's trade count, which independently confirms 59 was the truncated figure. That closes the Boss_16 bundle's lot-mode caveat BEFORE attach instead of during the demo. All 13 cases pass; added a permanent assertion that fails if the clean leg is ever itself truncated. Side benefit proving ORDER-219 end to end: the sidecars written by this run carry their full reason inline with no recovery step, so the 6>&1 fix works on new runs and not only retroactively

Tested whether NuiIndy's CutLoss_Percent=30 - the only thing between an uncapped-ruin martingale and a wipeout on a real-money account - actually cuts. It does, and it is not insurance. Proof is behavioural and exact: the cut30 and cut100 arms share their first 123 deals and diverge at deal 124, where 14 positions close together and balance moves 10521.99 to 7363.31, precisely -30.02%. That signature repeats 8 times, each taking 30.0-30.6% of the balance AT THAT MOMENT, walking the account 10521 to 1326. That ladder is the finding: a percentage cut measured against a shrinking balance is a ratchet, not a floor, which is how the run reached 87.29% equity drawdown WHILE a 30 threshold was active. Same year, same window, 4x sizing: +51% with the cut off, -86% with it on. The previously documented DD bounded ~15% was the switch never engaging, not a bound - free was true only in the sense that a switch doing nothing is free. The shape of the cost is the real lesson and it is inverted: never fires at live sizing (costs nothing, protects nothing), costs about 12% of profit where drawdown grazes the line with DD unchanged (genuinely cheap), catastrophic where it fires repeatedly. A guardrail cheapest exactly where it is useless and ruinous exactly where it is called upon. Also settled a recon finding: both archived runs wrote the numeric Leverage form the tester silently ignores and executed at 1:2000 instead of 1:100, but re-running at a verified 1:100 reproduced them (PF 1.17 vs 1.19, 933 trades in both), so the 20x error did not corrupt that evidence - identical trade counts mean margin was never a constraint at either setting. Took a blind Codex second opinion as doctrine requires for uncaged real-money risk logic, explicitly asking it to argue that I was misreading the data; it confirmed the balance ladder independently and corrected two of my figures (loss clusters are -573 to -3159 including swap, not -1158 to -3048 from profit alone; and the cut100 report is byte-identical to the stage-1 run, so it is a reproducibility check and not a second control - notable against ORDER-221, the tester is deterministic even though the compiler is not). Stated plainly what is NOT proven: the cut100 arm's only loss event is the tester's forced end-of-test liquidation in the final minute, so its +5088 is decided by the calendar rather than the market, which weakens it as a control for long-horizon ranking though not for proving the cut fires. Verdict is the pre-registered dead branch: revisit the value, keep the mechanism, because nothing at all is worse on an uncapped martingale - what would bound the account is an absolute equity floor that fires once and stays off, which this EA does not expose. No live change forced (the switch still never fires at current sizing) and the decision is the owner's: it is a user-mix account whose attestation confidence is none. Corrected in the same commit: scorecard row, EDGE_CATALOG (claim withdrawn, reusable lesson written), the ORDER-095 verdict (banner plus a strike-through at the offending clause rather than a banner pasted over it, per ORDER-214), and a first-ever EA_MASTER_INDEX row for this EA - it had none

Ran the standing non-FX screen as a real optimize campaign rather than a smoke sweep and it produced one candidate plus a strategy-level verdict. Six cells measured on Model-4: XAUUSD H4 1.51/1.03, BTCUSD H4 1.59/1.35, BTCUSD H1 1.23/1.04, US30 H4 1.55/1.01 (BWD net +2.91 over three years), WTI H4 no pulse at all (0 of 778 coarse passes survived), XAGUSD H4 thin at 0.6%. Every cell earns money in 2023-2025 and breaks even in 2020-2022 except BTC H4, which is a signature of the strategy and not of any cell, so the user hypothesis narrowed from non-FX suits SuperTrend to crypto suits it. Two levers were tested against a bar pre-registered before reading results (must improve BOTH windows) and that bar earned its keep three separate times: Donchian confluence took XAU MAIN 1.51 to 2.37 while taking BWD 1.03 to 0.48 negative at every DonBars value; the ER gate at ErPeriod 12 took MAIN to 2.405 with BWD at 0.838 negative; and the sensitivity fan later suggested Mult 2.0, which delivered MAIN 3.542 against 2.379 but BWD 3.307 against 4.044, so the prettier number was discarded by the tie-break rule win on the window we did not tune. The symmetry across symbols is the reusable finding: on XAU a long ER window fits MAIN and kills BWD, on BTC a long ER window fits BWD and kills MAIN, so filter window length is the axis that converts a filter into a curve fit regardless of instrument. Kaufman ER was ported into rev02 and a capped pyramid into rev03, both additive and default-off, with regression cages proving rev01 equals rev02 equals rev03-pyramid-off to the cent on the same lane. The winning stack is Donchian(20) plus pyramid MaxAdds=1: MAIN 2.379/50 legs and BWD 4.044/66 legs, and the config chosen was deliberately the least-leveraged point that cleared both windows because the depth surface is monotone, which measures leverage rather than edge. Cage completed: MC ruin 0 percent with PF-5th 1.114, worst single leg -69.50 or 0.70 percent of a 10k account against a 15 percent doctrine bar, fan 69 of 81 clearing both windows with BWD never below 1.71, correlation +0.167 against the live BRK_XAU money leg. Then the user asked to fix swap before spending the holdout, which turned a piece of lab lore into a measurement: BTCUSD is SYMBOL_SWAP_MODE_INTEREST_CURRENT and the tester charges nothing for it (30-day hold returned exactly the price-only P&L), while XAUUSD is POINTS mode and IS charged (-29.25 measured against -29.19 expected), so every XAU backtest in the lab already carries its financing cost and only crypto was overstated. Applying -14.67 percent per year against real per-leg holding time (mean 4.6 days, not the long holds I had feared) cost 51.79 on MAIN and 16.12 on BWD, taking PF to 2.257 and 3.949 and MC PF-5th to 1.052, all still clearing. The 2026H1 holdout was then spent once with no further tuning: PF 4.32 or 4.274 swap-adjusted on 9 legs, +250.52, eqDD 2.52 percent, 29.4M ticks, traded through to 2026.06.30 including a profitable short basket. Verdict VALIDATED CANDIDATE with the demo-attach decision left to the user. What must travel with those numbers: legs are not independent samples (34 signals produced 50 legs), holdout n=9 cannot confirm the size of the edge only that it does not contradict, both halves of 2025 LOSE (0.40 and 0.44) exactly as the ungated baseline did (0.24 and 0.36) which means the overlay amplifies whatever the regime gives and does not repair a hostile one, and the one unclosed risk is a weekend gap through both legs trail stops at once which the tester does not simulate. Two infrastructure findings fell out: BTCUSD tick history differs between MT5 installs so every crypto A/B must run on one lane (this invalidated my first BWD 1.35 to 3.51 claim, which compared across lanes and only survived re-running by luck), and select_robust_pass.py reported the 81-cell fan as survivors=0 plateau=NONE while the raw rows were profitable almost everywhere, so its survivor filter cannot be trusted on basket or pyramid result sets. Also corrected mid-flight: the merged matrix templates specified MAIN as 2023.07-2026.07, which would have eaten the same 2026H1 holdout this order later spent deliberately.

Resolved the cut-loss question the interim finding left open for MatchaGrid, a real-money grid EA (magic 20240001). Built the same deliberately-raise-the-risk probe used on NuiIndy, adapted to this EA's lever: no prior ini for this EA had ever pinned the InpCutLoss family explicitly, so every archived report including the one behind the scorecard's 2.08 inherited those five values from whatever the terminal's per-EA input cache happened to hold - pinned all fifteen known inputs explicitly to close that gap. Stage 0 tried to reproduce the archived control report and could not (PF 1.77 vs 2.08, 14x more ticks for the identical window) because the primary tester was occupied by another session and the run went to the parallel Meta 5b instance instead, whose CHFJPY tick history has apparently diverged from the primary's - flagged as its own integrity item, separate from and not weakening the cut-loss finding, since stages 1 and 2 only compare arms against each other on the same instance. Stage 1 tightened the grid spacing until equity drawdown reached 63.94% at 66 simultaneous open positions, roughly 2.5x the ceiling ever seen in three and a half years of calm history. The first pass stopped at the first negative-sum simultaneous-close cluster, which was the wrong bar - checked the actual balance before and after each cluster and found -0.63%, -0.27%, -0.19% and -0.19% of the prior balance, ordinary grid churn scaled up by the tighter grid, not a cut. Fixed the script to report percent-of-balance rather than counting clusters. Stage 2 held that same stress fixed and changed only the CutLoss thresholds, the live 10 percent and 50 fixed against an absurdly tight 1 and 1: the two runs are identical to the decimal, same 2961 trades, same net, same drawdown, same four clusters at the same timestamps. Changing the trigger by 50x changed nothing, which is the strongest evidence available without EA source that the mode is disabled rather than merely untriggered - the earlier finding could only say no cut was observed in calm data, this shows no cut is possible in stressed data either. Bounded-grid-plus-hard-SL is withdrawn as a property of the deployed config in EDGE_CATALOG, the scorecard row, and a rewritten EA_MASTER_INDEX row, the same withdraw-in-place-not-banner-patch pattern used for NuiIndy. Not filed as DEAD-STRUCTURAL: the EA's lot ladder is linear rather than geometric, which this lab's own precedent treats as a materially different and safer risk class, so the automatic structural-kill wording does not strictly apply and this is left as an owner decision rather than a lab-forced kill. Live sizing has never produced anything resembling this drawdown in the clean history, so no live change is forced today

Mirrored the skills library into git with a sha256 cage, since it owns every decision bar in the project and lived entirely outside version control. One incident and one rework, both mine and both worth keeping: .agents/skills is itself a git repo, so following the symlinks dragged its .git into the copy, and git stores a directory containing .git as a gitlink - a bare commit pointer with no content. The first commit therefore mirrored nothing while reporting 131 files, and I left it in history rather than amending. What let it through is the lesson: -Check passed, check_state passed, the file count went up, and every signal I looked at compared the LIVE library to the manifest. Nothing checked the thing the order actually asked for, which is whether the content is in git. Fixed by excluding VCS internals and verified by diffing the source tree against the mirror path-by-path instead of trusting a count. Also had to use .NET EnumerateFiles because Get-ChildItem -Recurse does not follow reparse points and 11 of 26 skills are symlinks, so the obvious implementation would have mirrored an empty shell and reported success.

Ran the missing Monte Carlo for TsMom 992001, ACTIVE on a demo account with an October judge date and dd95 UNKNOWN. The stale-binary detector was labelling 8 binaries STALE while 48 more were genuinely older than their own source graph and wore the advisory HASH_DIFFERS label instead. Single first-wins status slot, hash check evaluated before the staleness check, and the staleness branch guarded on status being OK - so given that MQL5 compilation is not byte-reproducible, which this same script measures and documents, any EA with more than one copy could never be labelled STALE. The staleness text was still appended to detail, so the finding sat in the JSON unlabelled the whole time; the blocking word is what makes a human look. Found by hand while checking prerequisites for ORDER-236, not by the detector. The masked set includes the entire Boss_11..18 chassis family, whose logic lives in core/*.mqh and therefore goes stale without the .mq5 being touched. Concretely the lane copy of Boss_14_GridLog was six days older than Inputs.mqh and covered neither lever the A/B was about to test - which would have made the two arms identical via input-cache fallback and reported a clean null. Fixed as a ranking rather than a rewrite, with a separate hash_differs field so the advisory signal survives. 55 stale binaries remain on disk, deliberately not swept: each needs judging against what evidence it already produced.

Swept an ATR buffer on the trailing stop of the validated BTCUSD H4 SuperTrendFlip pyramid and refused it on a bar written before the first run: better on both windows was required, and MAIN got worse at every buffer level, monotonically 2.33 to 2.19 to 2.15 to 1.82, while BWD rose. The order exists at all because of a five-minute measurement nobody had made: counting exit reasons in twelve Model-4 reports that were already on disk showed 116 of 116 exits over six years were stop hits and not one was a flip close. That is structural, not luck - the stop sits exactly on the SuperTrend line, so price cannot close beyond the line without first passing the stop, which makes the CloseAllOwn(flip) branch unreachable. So the exit mechanism this EA's own header calls the edge being tested had never run. The buffer switches it on and it works as designed, converting 18 of 50 MAIN exits into genuine flip closes, and performance drops - the validated edge comes from the accidental leave-on-first-touch behaviour instead. BWD moves the other way, so exit-speed preference is regime-bound in the same direction as the SuperTrend regime memory. A both-window bar refuses this correctly; a MAIN-only or BWD-only bar would have accepted opposite conclusions. Cost was one lever built and rejected rather than a demo slot. Sequencing lesson recorded against myself: I wrote a 200-line re-entry lever, had it reviewed, fixed four bugs and pre-registered its bars before spending five minutes measuring whether the gap it closes exists - and the measurement pointed at a different, one-input change. Parity was proven trade-for-trade, 100 of 100 deals identical against rev03, which covers rev04 and rev05 off-paths in one cage. Also found while writing the bar: mt5_montecarlo.py resamples by permutation, so PF is invariant across iterations and any PF-5th bar cannot fail - dropped from this order's bar and flagged for the ETH verdict that leaned on it.

The lane-collision guard had switched itself off and said so only in a NOTE. It printed no ACTIVE lane, 0 rows parsed, reserved-block and owned-path rules skipped, while the ledger it had just read listed three ACTIVE lanes. Cause: the row loop starts after the header separator and breaks at the first non-blank line that is not a table row, and someone had put an explanatory HTML comment between the separator and the first lane row, truncating the table to nothing. The person writing that comment did nothing wrong - prose inside a table is a normal thing for a human to write. What is wrong is a guard that disarms itself over it and reports the result as routine, which meant every lane committing after that line went in unprotected, mine included. Fixed in two layers rather than by moving the comment: strip HTML comments before parsing, so explanation can live in the table; and separate cannot-read-the-table from nothing-to-enforce, which had been printing identically while meaning opposite things - zero rows parsed while the file contains ACTIVE now blocks with exit 1, all-lanes-closed still passes with a note. Proven failable on three cases: real ledger parses three ACTIVE lanes and the rules resume, a table truncated by stray prose blocks, and a genuinely closed ledger still passes so the block carries no false positive. Found while chasing an unrelated hook message during ORDER-350, not by anything that was watching for it.

Order asked for one line: add _vps_deploy to the stale-binary detector default roots. Wrote the cage first and it went red on three cases before the fix and 14 of 14 after. The scope case reads the default Roots list out of the param block by AST rather than grepping the file, so the word _vps_deploy appearing in a comment cannot satisfy it - that mattered because the fix adds a comment containing that word. Acceptance met on all three clauses: 0 to 23 records under _vps_deploy out of 30 ex5, the other 7 being NO_SOURCE for bought EAs with no mq5 in the repo; the Boss_16 bundle came back not-stale as the order predicted from a hand check, though its literal label is HASH_DIFFERS rather than OK because a sibling copy exists and the compiler is not byte-reproducible, recorded rather than glossed since the bar said OK; and bundle-shaped folders with no mq5 beside the binary degrade to NO_SOURCE instead of crashing. The cage then caught a second bug that was not in the order: badCount was written as a bare pipeline dot-Count, which returns null and not 1 when exactly one object comes through, so a run finding precisely one STALE binary exited 0 and printed that every ex5 matches its source. Two or more reported correctly and the real tree happened to have 8, which is why it survived - the silent case is the day after you fix everything else. Fourth instance of the same shape in eight days after ORDER-260 substring, ORDER-341 label ranking and ORDER-390 nested backticks: the detector keeps working and quietly stops reporting. My own test then hit the same family one layer up, counting 1 for a 3-row JSON array because PS 5.1 sends the array down the pipeline as a single object while per-row assertions all passed. Opening the eye immediately showed 13 of 23 bundles older than sources that git log confirms were genuinely edited, not checkout-stamped. Deliberately not escalated: _vps_deploy is the staging point before upload, not the chart, so bundle-older-than-source does not yet mean the chart runs the wrong build, and what cannot be measured from this machine is which build sits on the VPS. Raised as ORDER-410 rather than written up as an incident.

Not a planned order - it surfaced as a wall while trying to land ORDER-370. The archive chain guard refused the move claiming the archive file was not readable at a 2026-07-13 commit, where git ls-tree shows it present. Cause was ORDER-270 optimization meeting .NET Framework: Process.StandardInput is a StreamWriter built from Console.InputEncoding with AutoFlush true, and AutoFlush true emits the encoding preamble at construction, so on a UTF-8 console git received a BOM-prefixed first request and answered missing. Three properties made it read as history corruption rather than an encoding bug. It is positional, so reordering refs moves the accusation to a different innocent commit. It is session-dependent, so the same code passed for the lane that closed ORDER-390 that morning and blocked mine an hour later on the same commit - the it-works-for-them shape. And my first fix was wrong in a way that looked right: writing to StandardInput.BaseStream with a BOM-less writer changes nothing because reading the StandardInput property is itself what constructs the AutoFlush writer, so the preamble is in the pipe before the first byte. Settled it by dumping the bytes the child actually received rather than reasoning further, which also showed it is InputEncoding and not OutputEncoding - pinning Output leaves the dump identical. Fixed by pinning InputEncoding across Process.Start, with a sacrificial-first-line fallback because that setter throws where no console input is attached, which is what a git hook can hand you. Cage written before the fix and proven failable on the exact fix line, 7 of 7 with the pin and 5 of 7 with only that line removed, and it pins InputEncoding hostile rather than OutputEncoding because the wrong knob would leave the test green on an OEM-codepage machine with the bug fully present. One case asserts a genuinely absent path still maps to null so the fix cannot convert fail-closed into fail-open. Chainwalk 11 of 11 and statusclass 23 of 23 unchanged. Lesson recorded: an error naming an old commit is not evidence that history is broken, and a fail-closed guard that gives the wrong reason costs more than one that just fails - it sends you hunting a problem that does not exist.

Came out of running /scrutinize on my own lane at the users request, which is the only reason it was found. ORDER-411 shipped a fix that worked end to end - the archive move passed - but chose the wrong shape: it pinned Console InputEncoding around Process.Start, a process-wide SetConsoleCP mutation, to solve a problem local to one pipe. It also leaked: if the getter threw where no console input is attached but the setter succeeded, the saved value stayed null and the restore was skipped by its own guard, leaving the codepage changed for the rest of the process. Worst of the three, the sacrificial-line fallback shipped alongside it was never exercised by the cage, because the pinning path always succeeds on this machine - so the code that would run only in the environment I cannot reproduce was the untested code, which is the ORDER-270 uncaged-cage anti-pattern wearing a different hat. Fix was deletion rather than addition: send the absorber unconditionally, verified by measurement to give identical correct blob OIDs under both preamble-bearing and preamble-free console encodings. One path, no global state, and it is the path the cage covers, about 25 lines shorter. Added a self-checking invariant that the first reply really is the absorber token, since a token that ever resolved would shift every ref by one - the exact misalignment the reply-count check exists to catch. Scrutinize also found the skip written as lines[1..(count-1)], where PowerShell 1..0 is a descending range and returns the row it was meant to drop; scope stated honestly in the order because with the absorber always present the reply is always at least 2 rows, so that case is now unreachable and the Select-Object -Skip form is defensive rather than load-bearing. The most valuable thing here was not the production fix: my own new test case for the no-side-effect property PASSED against code that mutated on every call, because I captured the before value at the end of the block after earlier calls had already reset the encoding, so before equalled after equalled clean. A side-effect assertion has to own the state it measures and re-establish the hostile condition on the line immediately before the call. Proven failable three ways afterwards: reinstating the mutation goes 8 of 9, forgetting to drop the absorber row throws on row count, removing the absorber throws on the invariant and shows the first ref coming back missing, which re-demonstrates the original BOM bug is live. Chainwalk 11 of 11, statusclass 23 of 23, and a real -Audit run exits 0 with both rebuilds zero-diff.

Nineteen arms across three re-entry anchors on the validated BTCUSD H4 host, all refused on a bar written before any number existed: better on both windows was required and every arm lost to the in-lane baseline of 2.33 on MAIN, so no BWD runs were spent. Best genuinely responsive arm was the stochastic re-cross at 2.20. The finding worth keeping is why one anchor could not be measured at all: PbAtrMult at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 returned identical results to the last decimal, 67 trades and net 535.96 each. The set files differed and the report Inputs page confirmed the runs used the different values, so this was the strategy and not the tester cache. Re-entry is only evaluated while flat inside a live leg, and the only way to reach that state is to have been stopped out at the SuperTrend line, which already guarantees a retrace of at least the band width - Mult is 2.5, so every threshold under 2.5 ATR is true by construction. My whole grid sat under the band width. Last-optimize above it, at 3.0 and 4.0, made the axis bind, 66 then 58 trades, still losing and converging toward baseline as the filter tightened. So the depth and S-R anchors were never actually tested; what ran was a degenerate re-enter on the first bar closing in trend direction. One rework counted for the grid choice. Reusable rule recorded in EDGE_CATALOG: a did-price-retrace-N-ATR filter evaluated after a line-stop exit is pre-satisfied by the stop itself, because the exit and the filter measure the same distance. Read together with ORDER-350: two mechanically unrelated levers, one holding longer and one entering more often, both degrade MAIN monotonically, which says this cell's edge is narrow rather than that two levers were unlucky - grow it with a low-correlation second leg, not with more participation.

Structural gap named by the second scrutinize pass and then closed. Every guard in scripts/check_*.ps1 runs on every commit via the pre-commit hook; the tests for those guards ran on nothing at all, because every suite under scripts/_test was manual-only. That is the ORDER-270 finding - a cage that never runs protects nothing - applied to a whole directory instead of one slow script, and it is not theoretical: four defects in eight days had the identical shape of a guard that kept running and quietly stopped reporting, ORDER-260 substring, ORDER-341 label ranking, ORDER-390 nested backticks and ORDER-370 a pipeline dot-Count that is null for exactly one result, every one of them found by a human happening to look. Measured every suite cold before designing anything, because the timing is what decides the split: statusclass 0.5s, order collision 0.9s, handoff contract 0.9s, blobmap 1.3s, versus chainwalk 74s, order101 about 120s, order103 about 760s and order105 521s. Built run_fast_cages.ps1 over the four fast ones, 3.8s total, and wired it into the hook conditionally so it only fires when a staged path touches scripts/check_*.ps1 or scripts/_test/*, which is the only way somebody breaks a guard; every other commit is an immediate no-op on the same idiom as the existing experiment-events block. The time budget is deliberate design rather than compromise: a hook costing ten minutes gets --no-verify-d and then protects nothing while appearing to protect everything, which is strictly worse than an honest four-second hook plus a written list of what it does not cover, so the script warns loudly if its own total ever exceeds the budget. Proven failable three ways rather than just run green: breaking a guard turns the runner red, a suite name pointing at a missing file reports MISSING and exits 1 instead of skipping silently, and the hook pathspec was checked to match cage files and to come back empty on ordinary commits. The commit closing this order stages scripts/_test and therefore exercises the new hook path end to end. Two things deliberately left open and written down rather than absorbed: the four slow suites still need manual runs, and run_order105_negative_tests exits 1 today on two real-hook zero-byte cases, measured before the hook was touched so it is pre-existing, undocumented anywhere in the repo, and split out as ORDER-421 because diagnosing it does not belong stapled to an infra ticket. Also recorded against myself: I reached for git stash --staged to test the hook pathspec and it pulled both the new file and the hook edit out of the working tree; recovered whole with stash pop, but on a shared worktree git stash is as dangerous as git add -A because it touches everyone work, and reading git diff --cached --name-only with the pathspec would have answered the question with no risk at all.

Closed on 07-27 by another lane and left sitting on the board until 07-28 because only the header was never flipped. The measurement itself is the value: ORDER-206 fanned _02_SlAtrMult upward from a base that sat at the bottom edge of its own range, so 1.37 could not be told apart from a cliff edge. Three runs below the base settled it - 0.93 at 0.75, 0.87 at 1.0, 0.94 at 1.25 - and with 1.01 at 2.0 and 0.90 at 2.5 already on record the whole axis loses except at exactly one point. That is an overfit point, not a plateau, and the cell that dies is GBPJPY times the SL axis, not the EA and not the XAU home. Cost of knowing was three runs; cost of not knowing would have been a demo slot and three months on a config that breaks the moment the stop moves. This row records the close, not the run: onboarding is NOT_RECORDED because this lane did not observe the 07-27 work and reconstructing it would be invention, and the evidence commit named is the header correction rather than the run, which is the honest attribution. The reusable lesson is about fan design rather than this symbol - a fan whose base sits at the edge of the swept range cannot discriminate plateau from cliff, which is the same defect ORDER-431 had to have corrected before it ran because its stated centre was the source default and not the value its own .set pins.

First optimize this home has ever had, and the ceiling came in at MAIN 1.18 on SwingRadius 2 - middle branch, so BUILD-ON stands and no BWD run was earned. Two pre-flight traps were caught before the first run rather than after: the lane binary was four hours older than its source and therefore did not contain the input one whole arm was built to toggle, which would have returned that arm identical to control and read as a clean null; and the source .set pinned neither gate, so the control was not a control until both were written in explicitly. The runner could not open a GUI Inputs page and verified from the tester journal instead, which is the better artifact because it can be cited later, and it flagged on its own that four sub-parameters were never pinned and arrived at source defaults by luck of a clean cache. Most useful finding is not the ceiling. The RSI gate returned exactly the same trade count as baseline, 250 against 250, while the long-short split moved from 79-171 to 66-184 and both gross legs shrank about thirty percent, turning a profitable arm into a losing one. A filter that re-selects rather than reduces is invisible in the trades column, so trade count unchanged is not evidence a lever is inert - check the direction split and both gross legs. The MACD-cross gate replicated ORDER-217s XAU result on a second symbol at exactly the point ORDER-217 predicted it would survive, a host with trades to spare: 250 became 28, so the participation cost belongs to the gate and not to the host. The pre-registered THIN rule discarded that arm without anyone having to argue with its PF of 1.53. Recorded against the register deliberately: scorecard and EA_MASTER_INDEX were not touched because this measured the second home while the deployed status belongs to the first, so nothing in either file became false and editing them would have manufactured a transaction. Accidental confirmation worth keeping: the re-run baseline reproduced ORDER-205s 1.08 at 250 trades to the digit on a different binary, which independently re-proves the ORDER-217 block is inert when off and shows the tester repeats exactly within one lane.

Seven Model-4 control runs on one pinned set to find a host whose BWD survives, and two hosts cleared the bar as written. Neither is usable, and the reason is a relationship rather than any single number: the two that passed BWD did it on 52 and 62 trades with drawdowns of 1.7 and 1.9 percent, while the three that failed carry 343 to 473 trades at 12 to 16 percent. The hosts that appear to survive the stress regime are the ones that were barely in the market during it. A grid taking 52 trades across three stress years at under two percent drawdown is not demonstrating resilience, it is demonstrating absence, and the n greater than 30 floor I pre-registered myself is far too low for a three-year window on this chassis - it screens out no trades at all, not too few trades to interpret. Both qualifying hosts then came back under 1.0 on MAIN at 0.93 and 0.95, so an overlay delta measured there could not be separated from simply losing less. Answer to ORDER-236 is therefore that the caged lever pair still has no home, which the order itself pre-declared as a legitimate outcome, so it parks rather than dies. Read with ORDER-236 the chassis now has three legs measured on the A/B parity config and none clears both windows, but that indicts the A/B base config only and not the deployed demo legs, which run different sets. GBPJPY truncated at 2020-03-12 with a 93.5 percent idle tail and 24.95 percent equity drawdown; the truncation cage caught it and refused the metrics, which is the cage working. The runner attributed it to the risk cage hard kill and quoted a log line, and that citation does not reproduce - the named log contains no HARD KILL, no GBPJPY and no RISK lines at all, and neither does any other tester log or the terminal journal for that day. The mechanism is well corroborated from the other side, since the source message at RiskControl.mqh 380 matches the quoted format exactly, the 25 percent kill default sits right against the measured 24.95, and ORDER-194 makes a halt terminal so a permanent stop is the expected shape. Recorded as probable and explicitly not as observed, because a claim that a guard fired needs an evidence path somebody can open, and accepting this one would have banked the single piece of evidence this lab most wants on exactly the standard it is currently auditing others for. Process lesson for the next order: instruct the runner to use the tool that emits an evidence file rather than telling it to go read a log.

Dispatched blind to Codex and it landed the diagnosis: fixture drift only, the production guard is sound. The synthetic test repo copies the real pre-commit hook but its seed never created pass-stubs for the checkers that hook invokes, so a synthetic commit died before reaching check_experiment_events at all. check_order_collision entered the hook on 2026-07-26 in ad470945, which dates the breakage exactly, and check_handoff_contract entered later in b5d71e47, so both stubs were needed. Neither commit touched the suite and nothing makes the fixture track the hook dependency list, which is the shape worth naming: adding one guard silently broke the cage of another. The empty detail on suite-unhandled-exception was never empty - stdout is blank when the hook fails, TrimEnd does not trim the front, so the leading newline survived and the reporter printed the case name then the real message on the next line. Fixed with Trim plus a fallback that names the command and exit code when a child genuinely fails silently, because a counter that can lie is worse than one that reads zero. The finding larger than the order: the unhandled exception was a throw, so the suite stopped at case 15 and the real case count is 105. That makes it 90 cases, 86 percent, never executed since 2026-07-26 rather than three failures out of fifteen - a cage protecting a commit-blocking guard had been running at 14 percent of itself for two days with nobody aware. Verified twice on purpose under different machine states rather than once: with three MT5 terminals generating Model-4 ticks it returned 103 of 105 and exit 1, and on a confirmed-idle machine 105 of 105, ALL CASES PASSED, exit 0. The two extra reds are concurrency cases that had never been reached before and are load-sensitive, not damage from this fix. Deliberately not absorbed into this row: red-only-under-load is not the same as harmless, since one of them reports 144 of 150 events written and this repo's normal state is an MT5 batch running while other lanes commit. Split out as ORDER-501. Also caught against myself mid-session: I read exit code 0 from the harness and nearly recorded that the suite prints failure and exits clean, when the 0 belonged to the trailing echo in my own command and the real exit was 1.

User asked to deepen the pyramid ladder to 3 ATR spacing with up to 5 adds and an increasing linear lot. Two of the three mapped straight onto set parameters; the third is refused at init by a deliberate guard against escalating ladders, and after the result it never needed opening. Deeper and tighter moves the two windows in exactly opposite directions: MAIN 2023-25 climbs monotonically 2.33 to 2.59 to 2.97 to 3.28 while BWD 2020-22 falls monotonically 4.29 to 2.14 to 2.05 to 1.88, so the MAIN-best config is the BWD-worst one and BWD return per unit of drawdown collapses from 2.98 to 0.93. Nothing beat baseline on both windows, which makes the host's original MaxAdds=1 the both-window optimum of the whole grid - a shallow setting that reads like an untuned default is actually the regime-robust choice. The MAIN surface has no interior optimum either; at 2.0 ATR spacing PF keeps rising with depth to the edge of the grid, the signature of a parameter buying exposure rather than finding an edge. Model-4 deliberately not spent because BWD had already settled it. The control run is what makes the order worth keeping: layered on re-entry it looked like 2.47 beating baseline 2.33, but ReMode=0 alone returned 2.59, so re-entry was eating 0.12 of the MM's gain and without the control the upper layer would have claimed the lower layer's profit. I also had to correct myself mid-order - I called MM a real improvement and said to proceed after seeing MAIN alone, which is the exact single-window mistake the lab's rules exist to prevent, and my separate warning that drawdown grew faster than profit turned out not to hold at the grid corner where return per unit DD was 2.51 against baseline 2.16. BWD is what killed it, not DD.

Fixing ORDER-351 did not actually bring the lane guard back, and I only found that out because I reopened my own lane and noticed the hook's message had not changed: it now parsed 19 rows but still reported no ACTIVE lane. The status column was being compared whole-cell against the literal ACTIVE, but every lane annotates its status with what it closed and which commit, so the real cell reads backtick-ACTIVE-backtick followed by a parenthetical - never equal, and in this file nearly every row is annotated. So the first fix restored the table and the guard stayed off for a second, independent reason in the same family: human prose in a machine-read cell switching the guard off, first for the whole table, now row by row. Fixed by extracting the status verb with an anchored alternation instead of comparing the whole cell, anchored at the start so a note that merely mentions another state cannot flip it. Proven three ways: an annotated ACTIVE row is now seen where it was invisible, a CLOSED row whose note contains the word ACTIVE stays closed, and the real ledger resumed warning on the owned path. The lesson I want to keep is not about parsing - it is that I was one observation away from closing ORDER-351 as done while the thing it was supposed to fix was still broken. Fixed means proven at the far end, not proven at the line I edited.

User ratified banning cross-install number comparison permanently instead of re-syncing tick history. User ratified option B - give B1 the audited repair path regression_baseline.csv already had - so this closed as both a guard change and a data repair in the same pass, and it had to be both. The rules moved into a dot-sourced library that the pre-commit checker, the commit-msg hook and the new cage all call, because ORDER-421 had just found the ORDER-105 cage running at 14 percent of itself after its fixture stopped tracking the hook it copies; one implementation with three callers removes that by construction rather than by comment. Append-only moved to commit-msg for the same reason the baseline re-pin rule moved there the day before - it must read this commit message and pre-commit cannot, and blocking in pre-commit would mean commit-msg never runs so the hatch could never open. The genuinely new rule is the one the order named: the guard checked that bytes were only added, never that what was added is a row, which is how ORDER-280 vanished while every character was still in the file. Three things I would not have predicted. The cage went red on its first run against a bug in the library I had just written, a one-element array coming back as a scalar so Count threw under StrictMode, which is the silent-pass memory landing inside the guard written to stop silent passes. The new row-shape rule blocks every commit touching B1 while a malformed row exists, so it freezes the Contract D append rule repo-wide until the data is repaired - found by running it, not by designing it, which is why guard and repair had to ship together. And scripts/lib matched none of the fast-cage trigger globs, the identical miss ORDER-434 hit one day earlier with its comment sitting directly above the line I changed, so the glob list is the wrong shape and I recorded that instead of quietly widening it a third time. Correcting the ORDER-355 row appended one hour earlier in this same file, which recorded the wrong root cause and, worse, had already been turned into a task for the user. I reported that BTCUSD tick data on the main terminal was corrupt because the tester log showed real ticks discarded for 1438 of 1440 minutes and 214709 tick price mismatches, and I asked the user to delete and re-download the history. They did. The rerun produced error counts identical to the digit, which is proof the data was never the variable. One short-window run settled it: six months of 2025 generated 32473873 ticks and 1048 bars using 704 Mb, while the three-year window needed 1984 Mb against a ceiling of about 2000 and returned zero ticks and zero bars. Three years of BTC ticks want roughly 4 GB and the agent has 2, so the tester silently returns nothing instead of reporting that it ran out of memory - the same misreporting family as the known no-disk-space-is-really-memory trap. The discarded and mismatch lines are level-3 per-day warnings that appear in successful runs too; the lines that actually explained the outcome were the two memory numbers printed just below them. I picked the scariest line in the log rather than the line that could account for the result, and zero bars was the result needing an account. Fix is to slice Model 4 by year and aggregate PF from summed gross profit and gross loss, noting that drawdown cannot be chained across slices because the equity path breaks. The cost was not the wasted runs, it was sending the user to do unnecessary work on my misreading - I hold the rule that a tool returning zero must be diagnosed before it is believed, but I had been applying it to other agents' claims rather than to my own before handing out a task.

Deep pyramid plus ER regime gate on BTC H4: AddAtAtr 1.0, MaxAdds 7, ErMin 0.25. Under real ticks the config holds both windows - MAIN 89 trades PF 3.99, BWD 121 trades PF 1.89, largest loss identical to baseline on MAIN, and Model 1 versus Model 4 differ by under one percent with matching trade counts, so no model-switch cliff. The holdout was pre-registered and committed before the run, then came back refusing the question I asked. I had assumed 2026H1 would be a non-trend window because 2025 was negative, so I reframed the holdout to test whether the gate stands down, with three criteria. Two failed: sixteen trades against a bar of twelve, and gate-on identical to gate-off in every digit, meaning the gate blocked nothing. But they failed because the window was a trend regime, not because the config misbehaved - and judged against the lab's standing holdout bar, which was never withdrawn, PF 4.02 out of sample passes. I also told the user it was highly likely the holdout would fail PF 1.2, which was extrapolating a regime call from a single year, and it nearly argued us out of firing the holdout at all. The unresolved item is the one the user's whole thesis rests on: the gate has never been shown to stand down correctly out of sample. It cuts trades on BWD and halves drawdown there, but BWD is the window its threshold was tuned on; on MAIN it cuts two of ninety-one and here it cuts zero. Only a real non-trend regime on demo forward can settle it. Two reworks: the first grid spanned 2.0-4.0 ATR with the answer sitting at 1.0 outside it, and ORDER-352 was closed on that grid's edge-of-range reading as if it were structural; and ErMin 0.30 maximised PF but sat one step from a cliff that costs 47 percent, so 0.25 was taken instead - the robust part of the gate's benefit turned out to be threshold-independent anyway.

Closed on measurement rather than on the user reporting the manual step done, which the order itself had insisted on. Closing ORDER-353 through Monte Carlo and demo attach. No Python exists on this machine, so I ported the MC to PowerShell rather than block on delegation - a second implementation of the same tool is a liability if the two drift, so it ships with a self-check that runs permutation mode and asserts the extracted trades reproduce the report's own net and gross to the cent, which they did across 210 trades at 2712.58. That check validates the parser without Python being present, and the tool now prints a warning every run that its default permutation mode holds PF constant, which is the trap that made a PF-5th bar look passed once before. Bootstrap results clear both bars: PF-5th 2.12 against a floor of 1.0 and ruin 0.00 against a ceiling of 2. But MC puts the 99th percentile drawdown at 2.89 percent while the tester actually observed 7.61, because resampling order destroys the serial correlation that produces real drawdowns - the observed figure is the one that goes in the record. On the demo side the important catch was structural rather than numeric: account 415573666 already runs magic 990025, the same SuperTrend concept on the same symbol, so attaching this as an independent leg would have booked a near-perfectly correlated duplicate as diversification. It goes in as an A/B partner instead, judged as one experiment, which also turns the pair into the only available test of the question the backtest could not answer - when a non-trend regime arrives, the gated leg should go quiet while the ungated one keeps trading. Two attach-time defects caught before shipping: the source .set carried AllowLive=false, the exact defect that left 990025 silent for three days, and the magic was still the 991006 test value. Binary verified current by mtime, not hash, since MQL5 compiles are not byte-reproducible. ORDER-510's deploy freeze was checked rather than assumed and does not apply - this EA includes only Trade.mqh and never touches the shared template core whose OnInit refusal that order is about.

The demo leg was attached and the screenshot shows it landed on account 463666728, Demo bundle 10 on Trial17, not the 415573666 I had written into DEPLOYMENTS.csv. Corrected the record to match reality rather than treating the plan as authoritative - there is precedent, TrendRider_XAU was overridden to a different account the same way on 07-23. The consequence had to be followed through rather than just noted: 990025, the leg this one exists to be A/B'd against, lives on 415573666, so the pair is now split across two terminals and falls under the cross-install comparison ban ratified this same day under ORDER-371. PF and net between the two legs can no longer be compared directly. The question the pair was built to answer survives, because it is a coarse behavioural signal - when a chop regime arrives the gated leg should go quiet while the ungated one keeps trading, and a doubling or halving of trade count is not something spread differences explain - but any claim about which config earns more is now off the table. Two verifications remain open and the row is marked ACTIVE-PENDING-VERIFY until they close: reading _06_AllowLive and _06_Magic back off the chart's Inputs tab, which the screenshot does not show, and recording the real first-trade date so the judge clock can be re-based off the provisional 2027-01-28. The magic is the more dangerous of the two because a wrong one is symptomless - deals would bind to an unwatched magic while the inventory points at one that never trades, with nothing anywhere to raise a flag. Lessons from the whole lane were written up as docs/LESSONS_ATTACH_AND_MEASURE.md, four sections, every entry backed by something that actually happened in this session rather than by what sounded prudent.

An EA on the October judge account was running the compiled default magic 990001, and the magic turned out to be the visible corner of a bigger fault: the bundle .set had never been loaded on that chart at all, so entry selectivity and trail behaviour were both off the validated config while the leg fed the judge. The previous lane found six differing fields but arrived at them by listing the keys it believed differed, which is how it first checked five and missed ExitMode. This close enumerated the whole file instead - 168 bytes, exactly nine keys, ASCII rather than the UTF-16LE the brief warned about, checked at byte level before parsing - so the diff against Inputs.mqh is provably closed at six and the miss cannot recur. Two verification traps were worth naming. The GlobalVariable Boss_990303_rc_peak_eq proves the magic took but not that the .set was loaded, because hand-typing one field produces the identical GV; that is why the order stayed open on the other five rather than closing on the magic. And the compiled defaults are current-source values while the running binary is pre-132, which the previous lane had reasoned past once already - testable here, since the five values read off the chart on 07-28 matched current-source defaults in every digit, so the assumption was verified rather than repeated. The user read the remaining four fields back at their .set values and the order closes: the chart runs the bundle, the re-pin was a real load. One earlier claim did not survive the close. Both this board and DEPLOYMENTS.csv stated the unpinned leg opened zero trades, citing the deals export, and the deals export is the file that refutes it - two rows on magic 990001, a sell stopped out for -0.98 on 07-27. The account snapshot agreed with zero for the wrong reason, because it lists open positions and the leg was flat by then; two sources agreeing is not two measurements when one cannot see closed trades. The re-base decision is unaffected but the wording is corrected in both files, and the leg is now known to have traded on the un-validated looser entry rather than merely to have been exposed to it.

Four EAs trading under half a closed trade per week were still carrying judge dates set by a bar that had been retired the previous day. ORDER-235 replaced the thirty-trade count for that class with twelve months live plus net positive, but no inventory row was re-based, and the inventory is what the judge is actually run from - so three of the four came due in about ten weeks against a criterion that no longer existed, and for the slowest of them thirty trades would not arrive until 2029. The finding that decided how this could be handled was not arithmetic but the type column. The originating handoff described the group as 991001 real money, 991004, 990205, which reads as one real-money row; DEPLOYMENTS.csv puts 991004 on 159503454 too, the same REAL_CENT account as 991001, so two of the three were real money and only one was demo. Taking that list at its word would have meant editing a real-money row unattended. The demo row was re-based directly and the two real-money rows were quoted back to the user as an exact one-field diff and applied only on approval. What moved is the decision date and the criterion behind it; kill_rule, status, start_date, magic, symbol and everything on the VPS are untouched, so the closed-drawdown kill keeps enforcing unchanged across the longer window - the weaker statistic is paid for instead with permanently small lot and no sizing up on PF. The two side-checks the order asked for both came back negative rather than being asserted: expectations.csv has no judge_date column at all, being the input that classified these EAs as thin rather than a copy of the verdict date, and the dashboard names 2026-10-09 only inside a comment describing the rollup, with the cohorts generated from the CSV and that generation independently enforced by check_state.ps1. A row reusing magic 991001 on a second account was deliberately left alone, its empty judge_date being correct because the lab does not certify that deployment.

ORDER-222 had ranked NuiIndy's CutLoss=30 against CutLoss=100 and then disqualified its own answer: the no-cut arm carried a single -15300 loss cluster in the final minute of the window, force-closed by the tester rather than resolved by the market, so a +5088 result had been decided by the calendar. This order re-ran the same A/B over eighteen months so the basket open at the end of 2022 would be settled by price. The ranking held and hardened - no-cut PF 1.98 net +44208 against ratchet PF 0.38 net -8495 - and the check that made it usable was reading every deal closed with reason end of test: the residual basket at the new window edge was four positions worth -8.63 and -379.72 respectively, under one percent of net on both arms, where ORDER-222's had been three times its net. The new finding is that the cage loses on both axes rather than trading return for safety: equity drawdown was 90.43 percent with the cut armed against 55.16 percent with it off, because cutting thirty percent of the current balance and re-arming against the reduced balance realises losses and walks the account down in steps. That is ORDER-222's ratchet-not-floor mechanism confirmed on an independent window and visible directly on the drawdown axis. Three costs are worth recording. The brief sent to the cheap worker told it to open a 515KB board file and died twice on context-window exhaustion before doing any work, so briefs for small-context workers must mandate offset reads. The probe script itself has a live bug - Invoke-Probe calls mt5_run.ps1 without capturing output, so diagnostic lines leak into the return value and a null reaches Add-Member, killing the script before the real error prints. And when that wrapper reported no report produced, the backtest was still running: metatester64 was holding 470MB, so a script saying it failed is not evidence the work did not happen. Separately, TaskStop killed the bash wrapper but not the claude-9arm child, which kept running, seized the MT5 lane my own cut100 run then aborted against, and committed on its own - I saw that terminal and declined to kill it believing it belonged to another session. Its numbers matched mine in every digit and are kept as a cross-check, but its cut100 figures came from reading the report I produced, since its commit attached cut30 artifacts only, and its claim that no cut100 sidecar existed was false. Nothing here licenses a change to the live account: this ran at four times shipped sizing to reach a threshold that has never fired at real sizing, and ORDER-373 settled the account question after the rule that would have reopened it was already in force.

An EA_BREAKOUT_XAU chart was running on the October judge account with no inventory row, and its log line matched the description on a real-money row, so the working hypothesis was a magic reused across a demo and a real account. The Inputs read refutes that and replaces it with something worse: the magic is 992017, which belongs to PivotBreakout_XAU, the strongest candidate in the fleet. Every EA_BREAKOUT-specific input on that chart sits at its compiled default while only _06_Magic and _06_AllowLive are overridden, which is the exact fingerprint of loading PivotBreakout deploy .set onto an EA_BREAKOUT chart - MT5 applies inputs whose names match and silently ignores the rest, and those two are the only overlapping names where the two EAs disagree. Nothing raises an error anywhere in that sequence. So the wrong EA was attached under the right magic, and since 2026-07-24 the 992017 row has been fed by a forty-bar breakout with a five-ATR take profit on XAU H1 rather than by the validated daily-pivot strategy whose funnel evidence the row carries. The order closes on the read it asked for, but its finding escalated into ORDER-530: PivotBreakout has never run on this account, which is separately confirmed by a complete untruncated Navigator tree and by the absence of its unconditional init print across 3747 log lines including a restart where eight other charts announced themselves. The Bars40 coincidence that started the investigation was, as the order own prohibition predicted, just the compiled default. Status was deliberately left ACTIVE on the affected row because choosing between ACTIVE and REMOVED encodes a disposition decision the user owns; the measured reality went into the notes instead.

A sweep to find which EAs on the October judge account were running compiled defaults instead of their bundle .set. The handoff supplied a tell-table and asked that it not be recomputed; used as instructed it was wrong in three ways, and checking it rather than trusting it is what produced every finding here. It listed two unregistered magics and one of them was in the committed inventory all along. Its ExitMode and SLMode tells compared an enum label to its own number, EXIT_ATR_TP being 22, so they carried no information. And its no-power list, which included the strongest candidate in the fleet, was an artifact of a scan that never looked at AllowLive - every bundle on that list ships AllowLive true against a compiled false, which is a decisive tell rather than no tell. Two instruments cut the work from thirteen chart reads to five. On a non-tester account a closed deal proves AllowLive is true, because every standalone EA here compiles it false and gates order placement on it, which cleared seven of the eight trading legs with no screenshot at all. And the VPS Experts log the user had already supplied was still extracted on disk; it prints magic and thresholds for several EAs, settling three more. The log was nearly read as empty: the files are UTF-16LE with a BOM and the encoding sniff tested byte one for zero, which is false when a BOM is present, so decoding as UTF-8 returned a confident zero hits across all three files. The instrument was then calibrated rather than trusted - three EAs known to be attached because they closed real deals appear nowhere in the log, so silence is evidence only for an EA whose init print is verified in source. Applied that way it showed PivotBreakout had never printed, which the user confirmed by attaching it for the first time. The reads found three faults. The 992017 row had been fed for four days by an EA_BREAKOUT chart wearing PivotBreakout magic, because loading a .set onto the wrong EA applies the inputs whose names match and silently drops the rest with no error anywhere. IchiADX magic 990067 existed on no chart while 990068 was on two, because the two slow bundles are identical except for MagicNo, so the wrong preset is invisible in every parameter that the tell-table checks. And Boss_16 had initialised twice on 07-26 and was gone from the Navigator by 07-28. Trade separation held throughout - both affected EAs scope ownership by symbol and magic together - so the damage was confined to the evidence the October judge will read. One claim of my own was withdrawn: I flagged the MacroGate chart as unregistered when it is the watchdog documented inside the row it serves, a row-shaped test applied to something that is not a deployment.

Twelve currency pairs Boss_14 GridLog had never been screened on, specified in full on 2026-07-25 and never run. The gate in front of it earned its place: in the lane the sweep actually uses, the binary was dated three weeks behind core/Execution.mqh, so all twenty-four runs would have measured code that no longer exists. deploy.ps1 turns out not to know that lane exists at all, which is why it drifts. The pre-flight's own method also had to be thrown away mid-use - it said to grep lever names out of the .ex5, and that reports every lever missing because .ex5 is packed; the sanity token is what proved the instrument wrong rather than the binary, and without it the whole tranche would have been blocked on a false reading. The screen itself came back with a pattern larger than any single cell: the grid arm is worse than or equal to the flat-lot arm on seven of twelve pairs, so the claim that this EA travels across pairs is weaker than the order it came from assumed. Two cells are ENGINE-EDGE class under the carve-out that retired the flat-lot auto-kill - AUDUSD and USDCAD, the latter at PF 1.25 over 242 trades with 8 percent drawdown - and neither has passed anything yet, because that class requires the 2020-22 window as a hard gate and it has not been run. One clean entry-edge with a real sample on both arms, CHFJPY. The order's own labelling rule produced two false positives and had to be overridden by hand: it calls anything at PF 1.2 an entry edge, which promoted a cell that took three trades in three years at PF 3.39. That is the participation problem the verdict gate already flags as unratified, and this is fresh evidence for it - the thirty-trade floor was not even enforced here.

BOX 1a of the S13C handoff, ratified by the owner before this lane opened. MetricRef required pf as a number, and one pilot cell - USDJPY H1, 99 trades, 99 winners, gross_loss zero - has a profit factor with no denominator, so it could only be registered by writing a number that is not true. The tester prints 0 there and ORDER-1230 had already had to repair that exact inversion, where the best win rate in the matrix rendered as the worst result in it. pf is nullable now and a required pf_state enum travels with it, bound in both directions, with a control showing all three new negatives validate again the moment the conditional is removed. Registering the 16 cells then turned factory/coverage.jsonl into a two-population store and every reader of it had to be taught the partition: the renderer projects imported rows only and states the native count rather than dropping it silently, a record that is neither is a ToolFailure rather than a skip, A2 counts imported rows only so that adding pilot cells cannot mask the deletion of an imported one, and A3 routes native rows to an allowlist read from the schema rather than to the imported-row key list, because FORBIDDEN_KEYS contains pf and MetricRef.pf is a measurement the schema will not accept without its provenance beside it. Four defects were found in this order's own work, three of them by the repo's own cages rather than by review. The verdict-value scan was an equality test, which can essentially never fire against free text - the attack that exposed it put a verdict inside a NOT_APPLICABLE reason and walked straight past. A3 read schemas.json while the store was injected, so the mutation suite ran a worktree store against an indexed contract and every control went red, which is the mixed-vintage verdict that same file records paying for twice. run_guard_shape_lint refused the new read for having no snapshot declaration, which is how that was found. And two files picked up a UTF-8 BOM from a PowerShell rewrite, which killed a whole suite with exit -1 rather than a named failure. Three checklist items stopped being stubs (4 PASS to 6 PASS), and more useful than the count, item 7 moved from checker-not-implemented to awaiting-evidence: all 16 cells sit at BASELINE_RUN and the state machine now makes it mechanically impossible to tick that item from the flat-lot arm, which is H01's falsifier and not the decision-13 optimize probe. No EA verdict is issued or implied.

The enforcement check in check_schema_structure.py opened with a continue on any entity carrying no x-enforced-by, so an entity that LOST its declaration left the check entirely rather than reddening it. Thirteen of twenty-nine were in that state and nothing held an inventory of which entities must carry one, which means a constraint and its enforcement metadata could be deleted together and the lint still printed STRUCTURE OK. OwnerRef was one of the thirteen, which is exactly why ORDER-1263 stayed invisible. The absence is a classification now rather than a silence: two closed sets whose union must equal the schema in both directions, so a new entity is red until someone puts it in one and a rename leaves a red stale entry. The second set is named for what it is and does not assert those entities need no declaration, because several demonstrably do, and writing a true one for each means auditing its enforcer one at a time, which is ORDER-1280. The completeness assertion caught its own author on its first run, naming OwnerRef, which I had left out of both sets. The control is the part worth keeping: each new mutation was run against git show HEAD of the checker and four of the five were green before the fix, while the fifth was already red for a different reason and the suite now says so instead of letting it read as a fifth catch. A delete-an-entity case was deliberately not shipped because deleting a routed entity crashes the branch check with a KeyError before the inventory assertion is reached, so it would have been green for the wrong reason; a rename reaches it and exercises both directions. OwnerRef is the pin primitive the whole ownership discipline rests on and its validator contained no resolution primitive at all - no rev-parse, no subprocess, no git, no open. Three blind reads found that in one day and the third produced the reproducer that ends the argument: an authorization_ref whose path is VISION.md, whose blob_oid is PROJECT_STATE.md s, and whose raw_sha256 is unrelated to either, accepted on a CANDIDATE_ASSIGNED event, which is the one event type that exists to require a human decision before a candidate reaches a live deployment. So the S10 acceptance that no non-OBSERVED event may be appended without a human authorization ref was satisfied by a reference whose three fields identified three different documents. Four rules now, named so a failure reads: the commit and path resolve to a blob, that blob is the one blob_oid names, sha256 over the raw bytes matches, and the anchor has no spaces and occurs exactly once - the last being a rule the schema states in prose on the field and nothing had ever read. The control is measured rather than asserted: all five attacks were accepted by the pre-fix validator, checked by running each against git show HEAD of the module. The fixtures turned out to be the other half of the defect, pinning forty b characters and forty c characters, which is a pin that proves a regex exists and is green whether the resolver works or is absent; they derive real objects from HEAD now, so they cannot rot the way pasted oids do, and the two anchor cases derive a once-only and a twice-over token from the pinned blob rather than hardcoding one. Cost decided the design: the live stores hold 234 refs across three distinct commit-and-path targets with 232 of them the same one, and the first working version took 11.54 seconds because it ran one cat-file per reference; content-addressed caches at both levels take the same 234 refs to 0.30 seconds and all of them resolve. The read goes through the evidence source rather than a second git implementation inside the validator, and it distinguishes a pin that does not resolve from a repository that could not hold the answer, because in a shallow clone those two are indistinguishable and merging them would redden a healthy repo the first time it runs somewhere new. OwnerRef moved into the declared inventory in this commit and not one earlier, which is the sequencing ORDER-1264 was built to make possible, and it is labelled BUILT rather than WIRED because nothing on the commit path sweeps the live stores yet - claiming otherwise would be the false governance state that whole split exists to end.

So the defect was never that no such check exists; it was that the one place a configuration reaches the evidence store was judged by a weaker rule in a different file, which is the built-not-wired shape, and adding a second implementation in candidate.py would have rebuilt it with the copies swapped. The policy is one public function now with two callers. CandidatePayload gained build_tag because the full-surface rule is unenforceable while nothing names the surface it is full of, and Inputs.mqh declares StackMode eight times, once per build tag; the schema change cost zero data because the candidates directory does not exist yet. The cage attacks the measured reproducer, the empty map, the surface minus exactly one input, an undeclared key, a tag naming a build this repo does not have, and a malformed tag, with a control that the real 116-input surface validates and with the one case a key count cannot tell apart, which is another build's full surface carried under the wrong tag. On the run path the rule is refuse-or-record rather than refuse, which is ORDER-700's reasoning and not a compromise: a compiled preset that no longer matches its own header is refused, an unreadable path is refused, and the 2177 legacy files are recorded loudly and never refused. A third launcher was found while wiring the two the order names and it was the worst of them: run_backtest's set reader returns an empty list for a missing path and prints nothing, so a typo in the set path produced a run configured entirely from the tester cache with no warning anywhere in its output. The cage pairs every attack with a control and was shown to redden on six one-line mutations, each naming exactly one case. Writing it removed a tautology before anyone could trust it: the first draft cross-checked its row count against pilot_probe_verify_xml, which counts the same Row elements with the same regex over the same bytes, so it could never come out unequal while reading as cross-validation; it compares the live artefact against the committed trial_count instead. Rule 3 of the ledger warns about exactly this and I still lost the race.

The guarantee ORDER-1250 stated in writing was enforced by nobody - one grep returned the generator and no other caller - and the store's own trigger ran the ACCEPTANCE cases, which read the store and agree with whatever it says. Both pre-conditions were settled before wiring rather than after. The read side moved through EvidenceSource because the module imported registry and not evidence and every read was a bare io.open, so in a pre-commit hook it would have judged unstaged files; --apply stays pinned to the worktree because it rewrites that file in place while preserving its meta and imported lines, and reading the index there would silently drop any meta line not yet staged. Cost was measured before placement and the budget stays pinned. The part worth recording is that the acceptance asks for a control proving it reddens on a one-character edit to a committed cell, and running that control for real - editing the live store and attempting a commit - failed twice for reasons that were mine. First the cage quoted literals out of the live store, so once the store was mutated the cage threw looking for a string that no longer existed and the tier reported it as SUITE THREW with the cause truncated; a cage whose fixture is a quotation of the repository goes red on the exact change it exists to describe. Every anchor is derived from the copied rows at run time now. Then the baseline copy was a photograph of the working tree, so with the store drifted the control case was false and the tier called the cage broken instead of reporting the drift - two questions riding on one artefact, separated by running --apply against the copy. That second fix exposed a real latent bug: write_store defaulted its path to the module's ROOT rather than the source's, so --apply with an injected source would have read a temp root and overwritten the REAL store; nothing had ever called it that way, so it had never been wrong in practice. The third attempt refused the commit with the checker naming the cell and both values while the cage stayed green, HEAD unchanged, and the store byte-identical to HEAD throughout. A cage that passes is not evidence that wiring works; the only thing that settled it was doing it to the real file.
